strengths: Novel integration of biologically-informed neural ODEs with causal structure learning that explicitly models perturbation dynamics rather than assuming static/steady-state distributions, addressing a real gap versus DCDI/DCDFG/Bicycle/NO-TEARS-based methods.
Demonstrates clear scalability advantage: runs on 817 genes and 1000+ interventions from the real TF Atlas dataset, where competing causal discovery methods (DCDI, Bicycle) fail to scale.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two SERGIO-simulated settings (yeast GRN, random DAGs) and a large real dataset, with multiple relevant baselines and both perfect/imperfect intervention formulations.

Interpretability is substantiated beyond simple visualization: recovered gene modules are validated against three literature-curated GRNs, gene set enrichment analysis, comparison to Erdős–Rényi random graphs with significance testing, and a biologically motivated worked example (E. coli flagella circuit) showing how the module structure maps onto known regulatory motifs.

Strong performance on the practically important task of predicting effects of held-out (unseen) perturbations, substantially outperforming linear SCM baselines in W2 distance and Pearson correlation, with supporting UMAP/PCA visualizations.

Reasonably thorough appendix with ablations (number of modules, L1 penalty, number of training perturbations), stability and generalizability analyses via bootstrapping and repeated train/validation splits, and detailed methodological/preprocessing documentation that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Absolute performance metrics (AUPRC on the order of 1e-3 to 1e-1) are very low across all methods including PerturbODE, and PerturbODE substantially over-predicts edges relative to ground truth (e.g., ~43,000 vs. 623 true edges for the yeast network, ~101,000 predicted edges for TF Atlas with no ground-truth edge count given), raising concerns about the practical precision and reliability of the inferred GRNs despite favorable recall/p-value framing.

On the real TF Atlas dataset, the strongest and most scalable competing causal-discovery baselines (DCDI, Bicycle) could not be run at all, so the paper's headline real-data comparisons are only against weaker baselines (DCDFG, NO-TEARS, NO-TEARS-LR), limiting the strength of the central claim that PerturbODE is the best method for large-scale real GRN inference.

In the simulated benchmarks where DCDI can run, it is competitive with or outperforms PerturbODE (Fig. 2a, 2b), so the paper's core claim of general superiority is only supported in the scalability regime, not in accuracy per se; the framing sometimes understates this.

The identifiability discussion in Section 5 rests on an unpublished, vaguely described companion result ('Authors, 2025') with informal, non-rigorous reasoning ('It in principle follows...'), which is unconvincing and reads as a placeholder rather than a substantiated theoretical claim.

Threshold selection for binarizing inferred GRN edges differs across settings and models via ad hoc tuning (different constants c, or fixed values recommended by other authors), which could introduce inconsistency into cross-method comparisons despite the paper's attempt to mitigate this with AUPRC and random-graph null comparisons.

Ground-truth GRNs used for TF Atlas evaluation are small, contain only positive edges, and evaluation is thus restricted to recall/p-value rather than full precision-recall, weakening the rigor of the real-data validation.

The stability and generalizability analyses show only ~50-70% consistency in recovered edges across bootstraps/splits, which the authors acknowledge is below a desirable threshold, indicating the learned GRN is not highly robust.

The impact statement is minimal/boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with dual-use or biosecurity-adjacent considerations relevant to inferring regulatory circuits for directed cell engineering.

Minor presentation issues remain (e.g., an incomplete citation for Hossain et al. 2024 with placeholder text '[source if applicable]'), suggesting the manuscript could benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: scaling causal/dynamical GRN inference to thousands of genes and large perturbation panels such as the TF Atlas.

The proposed factorized module structure (G = A diag(α) B) is a sensible way to reduce parameter count while retaining some biological interpretability, and the connection to known network motifs (e.g., E. coli flagella circuit) is a nice illustrative example.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive: SERGIO simulations at two scales, TF Atlas GRN recovery, held-out intervention prediction, module-level GSEA analysis, and appendix-level stability/generalizability/ablation studies.

Comparisons span multiple relevant baselines (DCDI, DCDFG, NO-TEARS, NO-TEARS-LR, Bicycle), and the authors are candid that DCDI outperforms PerturbODE at smaller/lower-dimensional scales, which improves credibility.
Considerable appendix detail on preprocessing, thresholding procedures, and hyperparameters supports partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: A central claim in the Discussion (identifiability of ODE parameters) is supported by citing 'Authors, A. (2025). Towards identifiability of interventional stochastic differential equations' — an apparently self-referential, non-peer-reviewed, or placeholder citation. Relying on an unverifiable/anonymized in-house reference to support a foundational theoretical claim is a serious soundness and scholarly-integrity concern.

The reference list contains other incomplete/sloppy entries (e.g., Hossain et al., 2024 listed as 'Preprint. Available at [source if applicable]'), suggesting insufficient care in preparing the submission.

Absolute performance numbers are weak in several settings: AUPRC values on SERGIO simulations are extremely low (on the order of 10^-3), and PerturbODE substantially over-predicts edges relative to ground truth (e.g., ~43,655 vs. 623 true edges on the 400-gene yeast network; ~101,404 predicted edges on TF Atlas with no known total). This raises doubts about whether the apparent gains in recall/AUPRC reflect genuine structure recovery versus dense, high-recall/low-precision predictions.

On the real TF Atlas data, evaluation is restricted to recall and a permutation p-value because only positive literature-curated edges are available; precision cannot be computed. Given the paper's own admission that PerturbODE over-predicts edges, this evaluation protocol is particularly vulnerable to inflating apparent performance without penalizing false positives.

Thresholding practices across methods are inconsistent and admittedly tuned per-dataset/per-method 'for clarity of presentation' or until 'reasonable results' were obtained (e.g., Bicycle's threshold of 0.005 was chosen because it was 'the only one yielding reasonable results'), which undermines the fairness and reproducibility of the cross-method comparisons.

Stability and generalizability analyses (Appendix A.13) show that ground-truth edges are recovered only ~50-70% of the time across bootstraps/train-val splits, indicating limited robustness of the discovered GRN, a fact that somewhat undercuts the paper's interpretability claims.

The model has many hyperparameters (number of modules, L1 penalty, thresholds, diffusion step sizes) whose selection appears heuristic and dataset-specific, raising concerns about how well the approach would generalize to new datasets without extensive re-tuning.

The Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate non-statement ('none which we feel must be specifically highlighted'), despite the method's direct relevance to engineering cell fate via TF overexpression, which arguably merits at least brief discussion of dual-use or misuse considerations.

Presentation is dense and paper relies heavily on a very long appendix (28 pages) for essential methodological and evaluation details, making the main text harder to assess as a self-contained, reproducible contribution.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: prior neural-ODE GRN methods (Hossain et al., Jackson et al.) cannot handle multiple interventions simultaneously, while causal graphical models (DCDI, Bicycle) cannot scale or capture dynamics; PerturbODE combines both capabilities in a single differentiable framework.

The model design is biologically motivated and interpretable: the gene-module bottleneck (A, B matrices), sigmoid activation justified via Hill-function equivalence, explicit decay term, and shift/perfect intervention formulations are all grounded in systems-biology principles (e.g., E. coli flagella motif example in Appendix A.12).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning simulated SERGIO data (yeast GRN and random DAGs) and a large real dataset (TF Atlas, 817 genes, >1000 perturbations), with comparisons to five relevant baselines (NO-TEARS, NO-TEARS-LR, DCDI, DCDFG, Bicycle).
Demonstrates clear scalability advantage: PerturbODE runs on 817-gene, >1000-intervention data where DCDI and Bicycle fail entirely, while remaining competitive with DCDI at smaller scales.

Strong held-out intervention prediction results (Pearson r=0.67 vs ~0 for linear SCMs; substantially lower W2 distance), supported by UMAP/PCA visualizations, which is a meaningful test of generalization beyond edge recovery.

Interpretability analysis goes beyond simple edge accuracy: gene modules are validated via GSEA/pathway enrichment and shown to recover known regulatory circuits (anterior-posterior axis, trophoblast, vascular endothelial programs), plus comparison against Erdos-Renyi null models with reported p-values.

Thorough appendix with ablations (number of modules, L1 penalty, number of perturbations), stability and generalizability analysis via bootstrapping/resampling, and detailed hyperparameter/preprocessing documentation that aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Thresholding methodology for edge classification is inconsistent and appears manually tuned per method/dataset for PerturbODE (choosing scalar c 'so that PerturbODE predicts a reasonable number of edges'), while baselines use author-recommended fixed thresholds; this ad hoc, asymmetric procedure risks biasing comparisons and undermines confidence in reported precision/recall differences.

On TF Atlas, PerturbODE predicts a strikingly large number of edges (~101,000 average, Table 3) versus much sparser baselines, but because ground truth only contains positive edges, precision/false-positive rate cannot be assessed—only recall and p-values are reported, leaving the practical usability of the inferred GRN (dominated by likely false positives) unclear.

The identifiability discussion in Section 5 leans on an anonymous, seemingly unpublished/self-referential citation ('Authors, A. 2025') for a different (SDE) setting, and the extension to the noiseless ODE case is asserted informally ('in principle follows') rather than proven, which is a weak substitute for rigorous justification of a core theoretical claim.

PerturbODE does not outperform DCDI in the smaller-scale simulated benchmarks (400-gene yeast GRN and 100-gene random DAGs), so the paper's advantage is essentially scalability rather than accuracy; this is honestly reported but somewhat undercuts the framing of PerturbODE as broadly superior.

The paper's own stability/generalizability analysis (Appendix A.13) shows only ~50-70% consistency in selected ground-truth edges across bootstraps/splits, below the paper's stated informal target of 75%, suggesting non-trivial variability in the inferred GRN that is not fully reconciled with the confident claims of interpretability in the main text.

Baseline comparison choices vary awkwardly by scale (Bicycle/DCDI excluded from TF Atlas due to scalability, restricting the strongest baselines from the flagship large-scale experiment), and NO-TEARS/NO-TEARS-LR often produce near-empty predicted graphs (Table 3), making them weak points of comparison rather than strong controls.

The Impact Statement is essentially a placeholder with no substantive discussion of dual-use, data-privacy, or downstream biological/clinical risks despite working with genomic perturbation data intended to inform cell engineering applications.

Presentation is dense and heavily appendix-reliant; several important methodological details (e.g., exact criteria for choosing number of modules, sensitivity of GRN estimate to the A·diag(α)·B factorization's non-uniqueness) are deferred to appendices rather than adequately discussed in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: scalable inference of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from large-scale perturbation datasets that capture dynamic differentiation processes, going beyond the modest-perturbation regime handled by prior causal discovery methods.

The proposed model is biologically motivated and interpretable: the factorized A diag(alpha) B structure reduces parameter count from O(d^2) to O(dl), the sigmoid activation is explicitly justified via the Hill function analogy, and the decay term is grounded in RNA degradation biology. The connection to gene modules and worked example (E. coli flagella circuit) strengthens interpretability claims.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple axes: simulated data (BoolODE, SERGIO at 10/100/400 gene scales), a large real dataset (TF Atlas, 812 genes), multiple independent validation GRNs (literature-curated human GRNs, ChIP-Atlas), and held-out intervention prediction against strong baselines (GEARS, scGPT, linear methods).

Demonstrates a genuine scalability advantage: PerturbODE trains successfully on datasets where Bicycle and DCDI fail due to memory/numerical issues, which is a practically meaningful contribution given these are the most relevant causal-discovery competitors.

Goes beyond point predictions with several forms of statistical validation (permutation/Erdos-Renyi null comparisons and p-values, FDR analysis, stability/generalizability bootstrap analysis, gene set enrichment analysis of inferred modules), which is a relatively rigorous treatment for this application area.
Extensive appendix with implementation details, hyperparameters, ablations (number of modules, L1 coefficient, number of perturbations), and compute resources, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Benchmark results are mixed and sometimes unfavorable: PerturbODE underperforms NO-TEARS/GENIE3 on the 10-gene BoolODE task and is outperformed by DCDI at 100 and 400 genes; the narrative frames scalability as compensating for this, but the paper does not clearly establish at what regime PerturbODE's advantages actually dominate versus simply not being tested (DCDI could plausibly scale further with engineering effort).

The identifiability discussion in Section 5 is weak and somewhat hand-wavy: it cites an anonymous/unpublished reference ("Authors [2025]") for a related but different (SDE) setting and asserts that identifiability "in principle follows" for the noiseless ODE case without proof, which undermines confidence in a core theoretical claim underlying the causal interpretation of the learned GRN.

The choice of thresholds/hyperparameters (e.g., c for the epsilon threshold, number of modules) appears tuned per-dataset and sometimes calibrated to match the known number of ground-truth edges or to match GENIE3's predicted edge count, which risks giving PerturbODE (and baselines) an unfair advantage in threshold-dependent metrics; the paper acknowledges this by emphasizing AUPRC, but several key comparisons (e.g., TF Atlas recall, FDR table) still rely on threshold choices with limited justification for generalizable ecological validity.

Absolute predictive/inference performance is often weak in absolute terms (e.g., recall ~0.35-0.5, FDR ~50%, AUPRC on the order of 1e-2 to 1e-3), and while relative rankings favor PerturbODE, the practical utility for actual biological discovery is not clearly established; no wet-lab or truly independent experimental validation is provided beyond comparison to other computationally/statistically derived reference networks.

The paper's own results show considerable instability: stability/generalizability analyses (Appendix A.15) show the model recovers ground-truth edges only 50-70% of the time across bootstraps/splits, which is not strongly emphasized in the main text and raises questions about the robustness of the specific GRN discovered.

GEARS, a strong baseline incorporating GO priors, outperforms PerturbODE on W2 distance for held-out perturbation prediction, and the paper's proposed remedy (incorporating gene priors) is left as future work rather than being explored, leaving the predictive-generalization claims only partially supported.

Presentation issues: heavy reliance on appendix material for core results (e.g., full thresholded comparisons, module interpretation, identifiability discussion sketch) makes the main text somewhat incomplete on its own; some figures (e.g., stability histograms) are difficult to parse without appendix context; the discussion section is very short given the importance of the identifiability question.

The novelty relative to existing neural-ODE GRN and causal discovery frameworks (DCDFG, Bicycle, Hossain et al.) is somewhat incremental—combining known ideas (neural ODE dynamics, low-rank factorization, shift/perfect intervention modeling, OT-based training)—though the combination and application to large-scale ORF overexpression data is a reasonable point of originality.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important problem: combining dynamic (neural ODE) modeling with causal GRN discovery from large-scale perturbation data, which is a meaningful gap relative to purely static causal-DAG approaches (NO-TEARS, DCDI, DCDFG) and single-environment neural-ODE GRN methods.

Demonstrates scalability advantages: successfully trains on the 812-gene TF Atlas dataset where DCDI and Bicycle fail outright due to memory/numerical issues, and remains tractable at 400 genes where several baselines break down.

Extensive experimental scope: evaluation spans simulated data (SERGIO, BoolODE) at multiple scales, a large real perturbation dataset (TF Atlas), multiple independent reference GRNs (literature-curated and ChIP-Atlas), held-out intervention prediction against strong baselines (GEARS, scGPT), and a large appendix with ablations, ER-random-graph null comparisons, and stability/generalizability analyses.

Interpretability is partially substantiated: the extracted gene modules are shown via GSEA and manual inspection to recover biologically plausible structures (e.g., trophoblast, vascular endothelial, anterior-posterior axis programs), lending some qualitative credibility to the model's mechanistic parameterization.
weaknesses: Core empirical performance is inconsistent and often unconvincing: PerturbODE underperforms NO-TEARS and GENIE3 on the low-dimensional BoolODE benchmark (Fig. 2) and is consistently beaten by DCDI across nearly all SERGIO and TF Atlas settings where DCDI is computable, undercutting the central claim that the dynamical formulation improves inference quality rather than merely scalability.

Reported False Discovery Rates on the ChIP-Atlas reference network are extremely high for all methods (50-58%, Table 1), including PerturbODE, indicating that even the 'best' model's predicted edges are barely better than baseline methods and far from reliable for downstream biological use, which is in tension with the paper's framing of PerturbODE as achieving strong GRN recovery.

The bootstrap stability and train/val generalizability analyses (Appendix A.15) show the model recovers the same ground-truth edges only ~50-70% of the time across resamples/splits, revealing substantial instability in the learned network structure that is not adequately addressed in the main text or acknowledged as a serious limitation.

Evaluation methodology raises fairness concerns: edge-selection thresholds for PerturbODE and GENIE3 are set post hoc via dataset-specific scalar multipliers of the weight standard deviation (different constants per dataset, e.g., c=1 vs c=0.1), while baseline thresholds are described as tried with 'no meaningful change,' making it hard to rule out that threshold selection differentially favors the proposed method.

The discussion of identifiability relies on an unusual and vague citation ('Authors [2025]... proved identifiability... in principle follows... future work could explore a rigorous proof'), which is not a rigorous theoretical contribution but a deferred, hand-wavy claim, weakening the paper's theoretical grounding.

Held-out intervention prediction results show very large variance for PerturbODE (W2 = 84 ± 88, with individual TF errors ranging from 66 to 300+), suggesting the model's predictions are highly unreliable for many perturbations even though the median beats several baselines, which is understated in the discussion.

Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the low-rank factor-graph structure echoes DCDFG, the optimal-transport trajectory matching echoes existing OT-based single-cell trajectory methods, and the module-based MLP parameterization is a fairly direct combination of established components rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Many key design choices (number of modules, L1 penalty coefficient, thresholds, diffusion regularization hyperparameters) appear to require extensive per-dataset tuning, which combined with the ad hoc thresholding above raises reproducibility concerns for practitioners without the original codebase and tuning budget.

strengths: Novel and biologically motivated architecture: factorizing the GRN as G = A diag(α)B through a low-dimensional 'gene module' hidden layer reduces parameter count from O(d^2) to O(dl), enabling training on datasets with hundreds to thousands of genes—well beyond the scale (50-400 genes) that competing differentiable causal discovery methods (DCDI, Bicycle, DCDFG) can handle.

Extensive and multi-faceted empirical evaluation: the paper benchmarks against six baselines (NO-TEARS, NO-TEARS-LR, DCDI, DCDFG, Bicycle, GENIE3) on simulated data (SERGIO, BoolODE) at multiple scales (10, 100, 400 genes) and on a large real dataset (TF Atlas, 812 genes), using several independent validation sources (literature-curated human GRNs, ChIP-Atlas ChIP-seq network, permutation-based p-values).

Demonstrated ability to predict effects of held-out/unseen perturbations, showing competitive or superior performance relative to linear baselines, NO-TEARS variants, and the single-cell foundation model scGPT, and reasonably competitive with the specialized GNN method GEARS.

Thorough appendix material including ablations on number of modules, L1 penalty strength, number of training perturbations, stability/generalizability bootstrap analyses, and biologically interpretable case studies (recovered anterior-posterior and trophoblast/vascular GRN modules validated by GSEA), which strengthens confidence that the model is learning non-trivial, biologically relevant structure rather than fitting noise.

The model formulation explicitly supports both perfect and imperfect intervention semantics and includes a principled decay term and diffusion-based regularization tied to stability/fixed-point arguments, connecting the approach to structural causal model theory.
weaknesses: Precision and false discovery rates are very poor in absolute terms (e.g., Table 4/5 show precision often under 1-2%; Table 1 shows FDR of 50-58% for PerturbODE at all threshold levels), which undercuts the paper's framing of PerturbODE as reliably recovering 'the' GRN—recall/AUPRC gains do not necessarily translate into a network a biologist could trust without heavy downstream filtering.

The identifiability discussion in Section 5 is thin and relies on an unpublished/anonymous companion paper ('Authors [2025]') for an SDE variant, with only an informal claim that identifiability 'in principle follows' for the noiseless ODE case; no proof or empirical identifiability check is provided in this manuscript.

Stability and generalizability analyses (Appendix A.15) show that bootstrapped/re-split training recovers the same ground-truth edges only ~50-70% of the time, indicating non-trivial variance in the inferred GRN structure across resampling, which is a meaningful reproducibility concern for a method whose central selling point is interpretable structure discovery.

Threshold selection for computing precision/recall/F1 across all methods (Appendix A.6.1) uses different, partly manually tuned procedures per method (e.g., c chosen so predicted edge count matches ground truth, or matches PerturbODE's count for GENIE3), which risks inconsistent or favorable treatment across methods and complicates fair comparison; the paper's own AUPRC-centric framing partially acknowledges this but doesn't fully resolve it.

In several simulated settings (BoolODE 10-gene, SERGIO 100/400-gene), PerturbODE is outperformed by simpler or non-scalable methods (NO-TEARS, GENIE3, DCDI), so the core empirical claim of superiority is really about scalability/robustness rather than consistently higher accuracy—this nuance could be stated more directly rather than emphasized selectively in the results narrative.

The linear SCM sampling procedure used for the held-out intervention prediction baseline (Appendix A.5) is somewhat ad hoc (hand-crafted noise injection formulas), raising the possibility that linear baselines are not optimally tuned, which would inflate PerturbODE's relative advantage over them.

Two neural-ODE-based prior methods explicitly discussed as related work (Jackson et al. 2023; Hossain et al. 2024) are not included as empirical baselines despite being the most directly comparable methodologically, leaving a gap in the comparison.
